lesson.title: tw → zw Openers
lesson.subtitle: two → zwei, twin → Zwilling, dwarf → Zwerg — the /ts/ costume party

hook.title: The Twins You Already Speak
hook.content: English has been dressing words in tw- for thousands of years: two, twin, twelve, twenty, twine, between. German took the same cluster and put it in a /ts/ costume: zw-. Two is zwei, twin is Zwilling (the -ling is the suffix of duckling and sapling), dwarf is Zwerg — yes, dwarf and Zwerg are the same ancient word, and neither language was willing to give it up. The German letter z is not an English z: it is always /ts/, the sharp double-sound at the end of 'cats'.

footnotes.title: Dwarf's Long Journey
footnotes.content: Zwerg descends from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz — the very cluster English kept as dw- in dwarf. High German hardened dw- into tw- and then zw-. So the fairy-tale Zwerg and Tolkien's dwarves are one people with one word, spelled two ways.

pattern.title: The zw- Family and the /ts/ Sound
pattern.content: zwei (two), zweimal (twice — literally 'two times', where Mal is the same word as English meal, the one hiding in piecemeal), zwanzig (twenty — the -zig is English's -ty, as in six-ty), Zwilling (twin), Zwerg (dwarf). The pronunciation rule is absolute: German z is /ts/, a t and an s said together. Two examples from the last lesson: zu (to) and zwei (two) both begin with the 'cats' sound. English twice keeps the t where German zweimal keeps both.
pattern.linguist_note: The affricate z [ts] is the word-initial outcome of the sibilant shift: ancient t broke into a t+s pair at the front of words, while after vowels it smoothed into s, ss, or ß (Wasser, groß, heiß).

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German word for 'twice' (two + times):
exercises.explanation: zwei (two) + Mal (time — the word in piecemeal) = zweimal.

exercises.prompt: Match each English word with its German twin — the zw- family, plus four guests from your TH → D and PF- shelves. Then recall earlier vocabulary in the short phrases:
exercises.target_answer: zwei, Zwilling, Zwerg, zwanzig, Zunge, Kleid, Monat, Darm, Pflanze, das Ding, Wir hassen das
exercises.meaning: two; twin; dwarf; twenty; tongue; dress; month; gut; plant; the thing; We hate that
exercises.explanation: Every English tw- maps onto German zw- in the native word stock — even dwarf/Zwerg. And tongue joins them: t → z turned tongue into Zunge, while Kleid, Monat and Darm carry their TH → D badges from the last topic.
The sibilant shift broke initial t into t+s. Zwei, zu, zwanzig — all begin with the 'cats' sound.

exercises.prompt: What English fairy-tale word is the twin of 'Zwerg'?
exercises.explanation: Both descend from *dwergaz — German hardened dw- to zw-, English kept the cluster.

vocab_hints.note: ein Mund — the same little word as English 'an', both from the ancient 'one'

exercises.explanation: Zunge pluralizes to Zungen, und joins the two — and ein Mund keeps its singular article.

summary.outcome: Read German zw- as English tw- and pronounce z as /ts/ in counting and ordering.
summary.takeaway: English tw- wears the /ts/ costume in German: zwei, Zwilling, Zwerg, zweimal, zwanzig.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the sharp S — when German writes ß instead of ss, and the letter English deleted.

twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Zwei Zungen und ein Mund" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of tw → zw Openers without relying on short-term echo.

zwilling.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twinaz (two, twinned) + the Germanic suffix -ling (as in duckling); English twin is the same root without the suffix. [wiktionary]

zwerg.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + K → CH
zwerg.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *dwergaz — German hardened the ancient cluster dw- into zw- and final g into ch; English dwarf kept both. Double-shift word. [wiktionary]

zweimal.etymology_derivation: zwei (two) + Mal (time, cognate with English meal — the same word as in piecemeal, "one piece at a time"). [wiktionary]

zwanzig.etymology_derivation: zwei + -zig (German's ancient -ty, as in six-ty); the whole word is a double t → z shift of twenty. [wiktionary]

zu.etymology_derivation: Initial t → z [ts]. Functions as both intensifier (too) and infinitive particle (in order to).

mund.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *munþaz — English kept the th, German hardened it to d. [wiktionary]

kleid.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *klaiþą — English cloth is the cognate: English th ↔ German d. [wiktionary]

monat.etymology_derivation: The twin of English month, from *mānōþ 'moon' (see der Mond) — th→d included. [wiktionary]

darm.context_phrase: Der Magen und der Darm verdauen das Essen.
darm.context_translation: The stomach and the intestine digest the food.

pflanze.shift_rule: P → PF / F + T → S / SS / Z
pflanze.etymology_derivation: Double shift: initial p → pf and t → z [ts].

wassermelone.context_translation: The watermelon is in the fridge.
wassermelone.etymology_derivation: Compound of Wasser and Melone; Wasser corresponds to English water via the t to ss shift, and Melone matches English melon, both from Late Latin melo. [wiktionary]

aufzug.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German ufzuc, a verbal noun of aufziehen, meaning to draw or lift up; the Zug element belongs to the ziehen root cognate with English tow, the t appearing as z in German. [wiktionary]

zwar.context_phrase: Das Auto ist zwar alt, aber schnell.
zwar.context_translation: The car is admittedly old but fast.
zwar.etymology_derivation: A contraction of Old High German zi ware: zu (the t-to-z twin of English to) plus wahr (true); literally to-truth, indeed, admittedly. [wiktionary]

walnuss.context_phrase: Die Walnüsse sind teuer im Winter.
walnuss.context_translation: The walnuts are expensive in winter.
walnuss.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic walhaz, foreign, plus hnuts, nut — the same foreign-nut compound as Old English wealhhnutu; the page names English walnut as a cognate. [wiktionary]

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Described by Walter Skeat as the primary dental affrication and spirantization of High German.
